Consummation
kon-sum-AY-shun
noun
From Latin consummāre (“to bring to the highest point, to complete wholly”) — the prefix com- (“wholly, together”) + summa (“the sum, the whole”); transmitted through Old French consommation. In theological usage the term denotes the final, decisive act by which God closes the present age and establishes the eternal order.

Biblical Definition

The consummation is the God-ordained completion of all things — the culmination of redemptive history in which Christ returns in glory, the dead are raised, judgment is executed, and the new heavens and new earth are established forever. Scripture frames the whole movement of history as advancing toward a single appointed end. Isaiah declares God's sovereign authority over that end: “Declaring the end from the beginning” (Isa 46:10) — not predicting but decreeing. Daniel's prophetic vision over the final week names “the consummation” as a divine terminus upon which even the great desolation must break (Dan 9:27). Our Lord's closing word in the Great Commission — “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen.” (Matt 28:20) — sets the church's labor within the arc of consummation: Christ's presence sustains His people until the age itself is gathered in. In the Apocalypse, the divine voice announces “It is done” (Rev 21:6): death abolished, sorrow ended, the holy city descended, and God dwelling with man in everlasting light. Reformed theology insists that the consummation is not contingent on human response but on God's eternal counsel. Election, redemption, sanctification, and glorification are all strands woven toward this one appointed end. The consummation is not the destruction of creation but its perfection — the body resurrected, the cosmos renewed, and every covenant of God fulfilled in the unclouded presence of the Lamb.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster defines “consummation” as the completion or final close of anything; that which brings a thing to its full end and highest point.

expand to see more

CONSUMMATION, n. [L. consummatio; from consummo, to sum up, finish.] 1. Completion; the act of finishing or bringing to perfection; close; end. 2. The end or final close of the present system of things; the end of the world or age. 3. That which completes or brings to perfection; the highest point or summit. 4. Death; the termination of mortal life. 5. Perfect or finished state; completion of any process or series of events.

In its highest theological application, consummation names the terminus of history decreed by God before the foundation of the world — the event in which every divine purpose and covenant reaches its full and irreversible completion in the kingdom of the Son.

Key Scripture

Isa 46:10 — "Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure:"

Dan 9:27 — "And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week: and in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease, and for the overspreading of abominations he shall make it desolate, even until the consummation, and that determined shall be poured upon the desolate."

Matt 28:20 — "Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world. Amen."

Rev 21:6 — "And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely."

Modern Corruption

Secular culture displaces the biblical consummation with utopian progress or therapeutic closure; liberal theology reduces the “end of the age” to a symbol of personal transformation rather than a literal, cosmic, divine event.

expand to see more

The postmodern academy and the therapeutic church alike drain “consummation” of its cosmic and judicial weight. Progressive theology routinely recasts the eschatological end as a symbolic horizon — not a literal return of Christ, a bodily resurrection, or a final judgment, but a “fullness of human flourishing” achieved through social engagement. The word is retained while its content is evacuated. What Scripture calls the “end of the age” becomes a metaphor for personal growth or communal healing rather than the literal close of history by the appearing of the Son of Man.

Against this thinning, Reformed orthodoxy holds the line: the consummation is an event, not a process; an act of God, not a human achievement; and its content is specified — bodily resurrection, universal judgment, the new creation, and the eternal face-to-face vision of God. The Westminster Confession (chs. 32–33) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (chs. 31–32) together insist that the same Jesus who ascended bodily will return bodily, and that the present age will genuinely close. To reduce the consummation to metaphor is to sever the nerve of Christian hope.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in Latin summa (“the whole, the height”) and the biblical Hebrew and Greek vocabulary of completion — the tēlos toward which all of God's purposes move.

expand to see more

Latin consummāre — to bring to the highest point, to complete wholly; lit. “to add up to the sum”

Latin summa — the total sum, the highest amount or point; root of ‘sum,’ ‘summit,’ ‘consummate’

Greek tēlos — end, goal, completion; used of the ordained terminus of all things in redemptive history

Hebrew kālah — to complete, to finish, to bring to an end; used in Dan 9:27 of the determined consummation

Daniel 9:27 — the word “consummation” itself appears in the prophecy of the seventy weeks, anchoring the term to eschatological fulfilment

Usage

"The doctrine of the consummation guards the believer against both despair at present suffering and presumptuous confidence in earthly progress — God will complete what He has promised, and history is not adrift."

"Every Lord's Day celebration, every sacramental administration, every prayer of “Maranatha” is a sign pointing forward to the consummation of all things in Christ."

"The 1689 London Baptist Confession devotes its final two chapters to the consummation — a witness that the gospel story does not end at justification but arrives at a final, unshakeable glory."
